- If sentiment is positive (≥0.25) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.20) and prices are trending down, model often overshoots downward; adjust upward slightly.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged flat or downward trend — reduce slope or add upward bias.
- When sentiment is high and prices are rising, model often fails to capture mean reversion; cap forecast at 1.5–2x recent high if sentiment >0.5.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 10–20%.
- If sentiment is low and true outcome is volatile, model tends to smooth out noise — increase forecast volatility or add 5–10% buffer for downward risk.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates near-term volatility — apply downward bias if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is high and model forecast is flat, it may be underestimating upside — add 2–5% upward adjustment if recent sentiment >0.4.
